card: This pull request introduces a vectorized ChaCha20 implementation using GCC and Clang vector built-ins to process multiple 64-byte cipher blocks simultaneously on x86-64 and AArch64. The change addresses high CPU consumption on the network thread during BIP324 encrypted v2 P2P transport, which strains nodes during initial block download and block relay. The author reports a 2x speedup on x86-64 and 3x on ARM NEON based on local benchmarks. This work is marked as part 1 of a series intended to later enable runtime-detected AVX2 and AVX-512 optimizations.
changed_since_previous: Includes a squash commit fixing namespaces and circular dependencies, with Lőrinc Pap now credited as co-author.

enables: Follow-up PRs adding runtime-detected AVX2 and AVX-512 ChaCha20 optimizations

evidence: PR description: 'Local profiling revealed that chacha20 accounts for a substantial amount of the network thread's time.'
PR description and commit e3386b9d0d: 'Demonstrates a 2x speedup on x86-64 and 3x for arm+neon.'
problem: ChaCha20 encryption consumes a substantial share of CPU time on the node's network thread when using BIP324 encrypted v2 transport, creating bottlenecks during high-bandwidth peer-to-peer activity such as initial block download.

risk.why: A computational error or state desync in ChaCha20 would corrupt encrypted BIP324 network traffic, disconnecting peers and disrupting node connectivity.

scope_notes: The implementation relies on GCC and Clang __vector_size__ extensions and __builtin_shufflevector rather than explicit SIMD intrinsics or assembly. It uses recursive inline template helpers to force loop unrolling without pragmas.
summary: This pull request adds a vectorized ChaCha20 implementation using compiler vector extensions rather than hand-written assembly or architecture-specific intrinsics. It processes multiple 64-byte blocks in parallel (calculating 1 to 4 states concurrently on x86-64 and up to 15 states on AArch64) when encrypting or decrypting data streams. Scalar ChaCha20 remains in place as a fallback for unsupported architectures and tail bytes.
